extracted.intended_audience: newspaper readers and editors interested in international affairs
extracted.subtask_description: News dispatches and front‑page reporting of international diplomatic and military developments during the Korean crisis, aimed at informing a general newspaper audience. Includes decisions about publication timing, prominence, and editorial handling of sensitive diplomatic texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate publication of diplomatic correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials said they had planned to release the correspondence when all replies were received; publication should be coordinated with the governments concerned (e.g., Ambassador Loy Henderson requested that publication be coordinated with the Indian government). Indian government officials called the publication of the Nehru–Stalin messages 'incorrect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay publication of diplomatic exchanges until involved governments have been consulted and replies are received; coordinate timing to avoid diplomatic embarrassment or diplomatic strain. Example: the American embassy asked that publication be coordinated with New Delhi and the Indian officials said they were awaiting replies from the U.S. and British governments before releasing the texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front‑page placement and prominence for major diplomatic texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages and important diplomatic statements were included at the tops/center of front pages and widely reprinted and broadcast (Moscow newspapers printed the texts at the top center of all front pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give highly significant diplomatic communications prominent placement on the front page to reflect importance and to reach broad public attention. Examples in the coverage: texts printed at the top of front pages, posted on walls and newsstands, and broadcast by radio stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral verbatim reporting of sensitive statements (avoid editorializing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers carried the texts of the statements with no editorial comment; the statements were broadcast by radio stations and presented for public study without accompanying editorial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing sensitive diplomatic exchanges, reprint the texts verbatim and avoid editorial commentary to let the public read official messages directly. This practice was noted in reports that the newspapers carried no editorial comment on the statements, and broadcasts echoed the same texts.
